Adult Magellan plunderfish attain a maximum total length of 9.5 cm [Li = 9.5 cm], a modest size that reflects the cold, nutrient-poor waters of the southern Patagonian shelf. Field surveys indicate that individuals typically reach the total length at puberty of 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], a milestone that appears tightly linked to local thermal conditions. At this size, females achieve a wet weight at puberty of approximately 5 grams [Wwp = approximately 5 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), measured during the peak spawning period, averaged 2.8% [GSI = 2.8%] at a water temperature of 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C]. This low index likely reflects the species’ relatively conservative reproductive investment per cycle, a pattern common among notothenioids that inhabit seasonally productive environments.

Embryonic development proceeds slowly under the persistently cold conditions of the species’ habitat. Incubation experiments conducted at a stable temperature of 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C] demonstrated that the age at birth, defined as the time from fertilisation to larval eclosion surrounding the chorion rupture, is approximately 122 days [ab = approximately 122 days]. Newly emerged, non-feeding prolarvae possess a wet weight at birth estimated at 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams], a value consistent with the calculated mass from an average egg diameter of 2.5 millimetres. This small initial size places the endotrophic yolk-sac larvae in a precarious position, as they must rely entirely on endogenous reserves until the mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding.

The lifespan of Magellan plunderfish in the wild is considerable for a teleost of its dimensions. Mark-recapture data collected over multiple years indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 3650 days [am = approximately 3650 days] at a temperature of 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C]. This longevity strategy, characterized by a slow pace of life and deferred senescence, is typical of high-latitude notothenioids that experience low metabolic costs at the ambient temperature of 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C]. The protracted lifespan allows multiple spawning opportunities across several seasons, an iterative reproductive strategy that buffers against interannual variability in food availability for the exogenously feeding, late-stage larvae and post-metamorphic juveniles. Field records consistently suggest that very few individuals survive beyond this age.

Adult females achieve an ultimate wet weight of about 35 grams [Wwi = about 35 grams], a mass that correlates strongly with the asymptotic length of 9.5 cm. This substantial body size is attained through a prolonged juvenile phase that prioritises somatic growth over early maturation. The length at puberty remains fixed at 5 cm [Lp = 5 cm], but individual variation in growth rate means that some females may reach this critical size earlier in the season than others, a factor that influences the synchrony of the first reproduction event. Reproductive output is size-dependent, with larger, older females contributing disproportionately to the next generation of recruits.

Comparative analyses with other members of the family Harpagiferidae highlight the relatively slow life history of Harpagifer bispinis. The gonadosomatic index was 2.8% [GSI = 2.8%] at 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C]; the ultimate wet weight of 35 grams [Wwi = 35 grams] was achieved at a total length of 9.5 cm [Li = 9.5 cm]. The persistence of the species in the harsh sub-Antarctic environment is facilitated by this combination of moderate fecundity, a long lifespan of 3650 days [am = 3650 days], and the ability to produce yolk-rich eggs that result in a 0.0082 grams [Wwb = 0.0082 grams] hatchling at a temperature of 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C]. Future work should examine how rising ocean temperatures might alter the delicate timing between yolk absorption and the availability of suitable planktonic prey.
